sources.title: Independent row-by-row arithmetic and source-identity derivation
sources.details: Dimension 0 is the token row axis; dimension 1 has two features. Contributions (1,1),(2,2),(3,3) land at rows 2,0,2: row0=(2,2), row1=(0,0), row2=(1+3,1+3)=(4,4). Assignment instead leaves row2=(3,3). Rows 1,0,1 place (4,4) at row1. Reversing the first/third contribution keeps the sum but assignment ends (1,1). Integer values are exactly float32-representable; this is not a general bitwise floating-point permutation theorem.

claims.statement: MoE dispatch groups selected token work by expert, and combine restores original token row order; multiple selected experts for the same token contribute a weighted sum rather than overwriting or appending rows.
claims.scope: General MoE data-flow mechanism; rows are token identity, distinct from expert identity. No specific GPU primitive or asynchronous execution schedule is implied.

evidence.supports: Router assigns token/expert weights, permutation groups by expert, un-permutation restores input order, §2.4 explicitly sums multiple weighted expert results for each token.

claims.statement: For rows [2,0,2], accumulated output is [[2,2],[0,0],[4,4]] and overwrite output ends in [3,3]; the row-ID and completion-order exercise predictions are correct.
claims.location: 15.6 arithmetic paragraph, Python fence and exercise
claims.scope: Three completed weighted contribution vectors, two features each, three token rows, zero-based indices. Exact hand/toy values only; not a general exact floating-point reorder guarantee.

evidence.supports: Exact sums and overwritten last values for original and two specified exercise variants.
The unmodified fence matches original sum/overwrite expectations.
Both original and specified perturbation outputs were asserted independently.

verification.expected: Original sum [[2,2],[0,0],[4,4]], overwrite [[2,2],[0,0],[3,3]]; rows [1,0,1] put [4,4] at row1; swap first/third contribution leaves sum unchanged and final overwritten row2 [1,1].
verification.details: Axis 0 is token rows, width=2 features. Values are float32-representable integers; no unit conversion, ratio or statistical denominator is involved. All entries were checked by torch.equal.
verification.tolerance: Exact equality for these integer-valued toy tensors.

claims.statement: The displayed grouped tensor API code creates a three-by-two zero output and index_add_(0, rows, contributions) accumulates matching source vectors in place on the row axis; assignment overwrites, and tolist displays the actual resulting values.
claims.scope: Grouped coverage: torch.tensor row IDs/float contributions, torch.zeros(3,2), index_add_ axis/index/source contract, integer tensor row assignment, zip iteration, and tolist nested output. The in-place method returns self, not a separately allocated output.

evidence.supports: index_add_ adds source into self at indexed positions along dim and requires matching sizes; tolist gives nested values; index_add is the explicit out-of-place variant.

evidence.locator: Original fence source line 196, captured stdout and environment
evidence.supports: All related calls execute together with the given dtype/shape and produce the displayed results.
The in-place return aliases result; reassignment instead retains only the last contribution.

verification.expected: All original API calls succeed; index_add_ changes result itself and returns the same object; assignment overwrites earlier contributions.
verification.observed: Original fence exit 0; return identity asserted true for all three variants; expected arrays match.
verification.details: Reference API tag v2.8.0 and installed runtime 2.14.1+cpu are explicitly distinguished. No assumption that the method returns None.

claims.statement: The formal MoEFFN finds each expert’s selected source token rows, runs only experts with selected work, multiplies by routing weights, accumulates via index_add_, and restores input shape using a readable Python loop.
claims.location: 15.6 selected-reading paragraph, first two sentences and dispatch/combine paragraph
claims.scope: Current and formal-source implementation contracts; not a dedicated sparse GPU kernel and no claim of measured acceleration. Only selected expert calls are skipped/executed; the small check is an untrained forward.

evidence.supports: torch.where gives token_rows/slots, nonempty branch calls selected expert, weighting and index_add_ restore original rows/shape; Python loop and regular FFN layers are explicit.
FFN result returns to same feature/table shape and is added via the outer residual path.
Six imbalanced rows choose only experts 0/1; observed expert rows [6,6,0,0] execute all 12 selections and output matches a per-token reference.

verification.expected: Six rows, top-2 produce 12 expert jobs; only selected experts are called, shape is [2,3,2], weighted sum agrees with explicit reference.
verification.observed: Calls [6,6,0,0]; 12/12 jobs; original [2,3,2] shape; maximum absolute difference 5.960464477539063e-08.
verification.details: Tolerance 1e-6 for float32 weighted reference; static method trace confirms no sparse GPU kernel or expert capacity truncation. Formal metadata identifies identical modern.py/model.py source hashes.

claims.statement: Dropless means selected expert work is not discarded because an expert is overloaded; capacity-limited designs need a separate overflow policy. The toy zero row comes solely from the lack of a supplied contribution.
claims.location: 15.6 paragraph starting 本例第1列保持零
claims.scope: Definition and scope only: the deliberately incomplete toy contribution table is not normal token dropping or a real full MoE route table.

evidence.supports: The proposed dropless computation never drops tokens; finite-capacity examples may omit excess work and sum/restore only received expert outputs.

evidence.locator: §2.2 equation 3 and paragraph immediately following, page 7
evidence.supports: Finite expert capacity may skip overflowed computation and preserve the token via the residual connection; additional buffer costs computation/memory.
No capacity truncation branch exists in this repo; all rows for each selected expert are processed.

claims.statement: Formal routing statistics and the training auxiliary objective exclude PAD via valid masks, while MoEFFN still performs selected expert work on the padded input table.
claims.scope: Formal wrapper methods and the corresponding recorded formal revision, not arbitrary direct stock MoEFFN auxiliary calls. No formal dataset counts or outcome scores were inspected.

evidence.supports: The input batch is right-padded to rectangular shape, with a separate valid mask.
Valid mask is not passed into stock FFN; the feature table includes padding positions.
Valid indexing selects real positions for auxiliary/counts, _forward replaces stock auxiliary, and formal training loss uses it.
The formal revision file hash matches the original metadata and these methods are AST-identical to current methods.
A 2x3 padded batch has four valid positions; all 12 top-2 expert jobs run, but statistics count 8 valid selections and masked auxiliary matches independent arithmetic.

verification.expected: Six padded positions x k=2 execute 12 jobs; four valid positions x k=2 give routing denominator 8; recomputed auxiliary uses only valid inputs.
verification.observed: 12 jobs executed, valid input count 4, routing counts [0,2,3,3] sum to 8; wrapper/manual auxiliary both 1.147748351097107, absolute difference 0.
verification.details: Only two synthetic examples and one untrained TinyLM forward. Auxiliary tolerance 1e-7; job/count checks exact. Formal current/recorded methods independently matched without reading result interpretations.

claims.statement: The auxiliary loss is an additional training objective intended to encourage more balanced expert assignment; correct data flow alone does not establish speed or quality.
claims.scope: Objective purpose and inference limitation. No guaranteed balance, performance improvement, full training completion or universal cost/quality preference is asserted.

evidence.locator: §2.2 A Differentiable Load Balancing Loss, equations 4–6 and following paragraph, pages 7–8
evidence.supports: The scaled dot product of dispatched fraction and mean router probability is added to training loss to encourage balance; probability component is differentiable.
Repo computes the valid-mask load/probability objective and adds the weighted extra term.
Sparse data flow has hardware/software costs; efficient execution is a separate implementation problem.
